TISSUE
• Groups of similar cells that work 
together to perform a specific 
function
• 4 major tissue types:
1.
Epithelial tissue
2.
Connective tissue
3.
Muscle tissue
4.
Nervous tissue
ORGAN
• Organs are combinations of 
different tissues that form a 
structural and functional unit
Heart
Lungs
Stomach
Small intestine
Liver
Large Intestine
Gall Bladder
Organ system
ORGAN SYSTEMS
• Are groups of organs that 
cooperate to perform the major 
activities of the body 
• The five main organ systems that 
we will be focusing on in this unit 
are:
1.
The Respiratory System
2.
The Circulatory System
3.
The Reproductive System
4.
The Digestive System
5.
The Excretory System
Organism 
• Organism: a complete, individual 
living thing.
• Examples:
A single person
A single plant
A single bacterium
A single protist

• Robert Hooke was first discovered cell in 1665 
cork cells
• Hooke actually saw the dead cell walls of 
plant cell (cork tree). No nucleus and other 
organelles
Cell theory
1675:  Antonie van 
Leeuwenhoek first 
observed living cells 
in pond water
1838: German 
botanist Schleiden
concluded that all 
plants are made of 
cells
1839: German 
biologist Theodor 
Schwann stated that 
all animals are made 
of cells
CELL THEORY
• Schleiden & Schwann (1839): Organism are composed of similar units 
of organization
Multicellular organism 
Unicellular organism
Modern cell theory
All known living things are made up off cells
The cell is structural & functional unit off all living things
All cells come from pre-existing cells by division
All cells are basically the same in chemical composition
• Cells are the smallest units that can be alive
• The individual cells can grow, reproduce, process information, 
respond to stimuli, and carry out an amazing array of chemical 
reactions
• Every living thing is made up of one or more cells
cells
A typical animal cell is between 10 and 30 micrometers (µm)
Plasma 
membrane
Cytoplasm 
Nucleus

• Light microscope
• Scanning electron mycroscope
Microscope 
• Ultracentrifuge to separate particles in cells
• Electrophoresis 
Cell fractination

• Regulation of gene expression
DNA 
recombination

Cells are able to respond to stimuli
Cells growth  (proliferation & enlarge) & develop (differentiation)
Cells Change Shape & move

Prokaryotic

Membrane

Prokaryotes: the first cells
• Cells that lack a nucleus 
• No membrane-bound organelles
• Includes bacteria
• Simplest type of cell
• Single, circular chromosome
• Nucleoid region (center) contains 
the DNA
• Surrounded by cell membrane & 
cell wall (peptidoglycan)
• Contain ribosomes (no 
membrane) in their cytoplasm to 
make proteins
Eukaryotes 
• Cells that HAVE a nucleus and 
membrane-bound organelles
• Includes protists, fungi, plants, and 
animals
• More complex type of cells
Prokaryotic cells have a simpler internal
organization than eukaryotic cells
Principal differences between prokaryotic & eukaryotic cells
• Organelle= “little organ”
• Very small 
• Perform various functions for a cell
• Found only inside eukaryotic cells
• Found in the cytoplasm
• May or may not be membrane-bound
• The largest organelle in the cellthe 
easiest organelle to see under a 
microscope
• A membranous organelle 
• Contains the cellular genetic material
• 5-10 μm in diameter
• The majority of human cells have a 
single nucleus, although there are 
several cell types that have multiple 
nuclei (e.g. osteoclasts, muscle cell) or 
don't have a nucleus at all 
(erythrocytes).
Nucleus structure
1.
Nuclear envelope
2.
Nuclear pore
3.
Nucleoplasm 
4.
Chromosome 
5.
Nucleolus
Nuclear envelope
• Double membrane: each membrane is a phospholipid bilayer
• The outer membrane is continuous with endoplasmic 
reticulum
• The outer nuclear membrane has ribosomes attached
• The inner membrane of the nuclear envelope is attached to 
proteins that are specific 
• The inner nuclear membrane is internally lined by protein 
filaments meshwork organised in a net-like fashion, called 
nuclear lamina lamin
Nuclear pore
• The nuclear envelope is perforated with tiny 
pores with diameters of around 100 nm
• Each pore is lined with a structure of 50 to 100 
different proteins known as the nuclear pore 
complex
• Regulate the movements of macromolecules, 
RNAs and proteins nuclear transport
• Active and passive transport
Nucleoplasm 
• Semi-liquid, fills the empty space in the nucleus
• Various proteins and enzymes dissolved
Chromosomes
• Chromosome  as a basis of heredity
• Chromosomes: containing a long DNA 
molecule which is associated with various 
proteins. 
• The DNA coils around protein complexes 
called nucleosomes, formed of proteins 
called histones
• The mass of DNA and proteins inside a 
chromosome is referred to as chromatin
• The chromosomes are copied, forming sister 
chromosomes known a chromatids
Nucleolus 
• When a nucleus is not dividing, a structure called a nucleolus 
becomes visible. 
• The nucleolus is a prominent sub-nuclear structure that is                                                        
not bound by a membrane and resides within the nuclear matrix
• The size of the nucleolus depends on the metabolic activity of the 
cell, with large nucleoli found in cells that are actively engaged in 
protein synthesis. 
• Eukaryotic cells often contain a single nucleolus, but several are 
also possible. The exact number of nucleoli is fixed among 
members of the same species
• Nucleoli is the site of rRNA transcription and processing, and of 
ribosome assembly (pre-ribosomal protein)
Nucleus function
• Control of the genetical information of the cell 
and thus the heredity characteristics of an 
organism,
• Control of the protein and enzyme synthesis
• Control of cell division and cell growth
• Storage of DNA, RNA
• Regulation of the transcription of the mRNA to 
protein
• Production of ribosomes
abnormality
• Nucleus abnormalities
• Wilson’s disease leads to an increase in glycogen in the nuclei
• Acute myeloid leukaemia causes nuclei to become cup-shaped
• Nucleolus abnormalities
• Hereditary disease
• Degenerative diseases such as Huntington’s and Alzheimer’s, 
cardiomyopathy and muscular dystrophy
• Laminopathies
• Mutations in the genes that code for lamins
• Autosomal dominant Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, Dunnigan-type 
familial partial lipodystrophy
• The cytoplasm is the semi-viscous ground substance of the cell
• made of 70% – 80% water and is usually colorless
• The outer clear and glassy layer of the cytoplasm is called the ectoplasm or 
the cell cortex and the inner granular mass is called the endoplasm
• Contains proteins, carbohydrates, salts, sugars, amino acids, and 
nucleotides
• Helps the movement of the cellular materials around the cell 
cytoplasmic streaming
• The cytoplasm is the site for most of the enzymatic reactions and 
metabolic activity of the cell
Cytoplasm 
• The main components of the cytoplasm are:
1.
Cytosol– a gel-like substance
• the part of the cytoplasm that is not occupied by any organelle
• gelatinous fluid
• consists of cytoskeleton filaments, organic molecules, salt, and water.
2.
Organelles 
3.
Various cytoplasmic inclusions.
• different types of insoluble particles or molecules
• basically granules of starch , glycogen, lipid and they can store energy
• Netlike labyrinth of branching tubules & 
flattened sacs that extend throughout 
the cytosol
• ER is a continuous single membrane 
system but consists of various domains 
that perform different functions
• Structurally distinct domains of this 
organelle                                                                              
include the rough and smooth ER
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
Smooth ER
• Is attached to the ends of rough ER
• Structure: tubular
• Smooth ER lacks ribosomes on its 
surface
• Makes cell products that are used 
INSIDE the cell
• Abundant only in certain cell types: 
steroid-synthesizing cells, liver cells
Rough ER
• Has ribosomes on its surface  
• Makes membrane proteins and 
proteins for EXPORT out of cell
• Proteins are made by ribosomes on 
ER surface
• They are then threaded into the 
interior of the Rough ER to be 
modified  and transported
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
• Synthesis of proteins & lipid
• The folding and modification of proteins in the ER lumen 
• Detoxify both lipid-soluble drug & various harmfull compound 
produced by metabolism by cytochrome P450 family especially in 
the liver 
• The storage of calcium ions and their regulated release into the 
cytosol
• Sarcoplasmic reticulum: smooth ER in muscle cells release & 
uptake Ca2+
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
• A Signal-Recognition Particle (SRP) direct 
the ER signal sequence to a specific 
receptor in the rough ER membrane 
How ER signal sequences and SRP direct 
ribosomes to the ER membrane
Free & membrane-bound polyribosomes
• The Golgi Apparatus is also known as the 
Golgi Complex or Golgi Body. 
• The name comes from Italian anatomist 
Camillo Golgi, who identified it in 1898.
• Location: near the nucleus & floating in the 
cytoplasm
• It is part of the endomembrane system. 
Golgi apparatus 
• Cisternae (about 1 μm in diameter) are central, 
flattened, plate-like closed compartments that 
are held in stacks one above the other
• The vesicles (60 nm in diameter) are of three 
types:
1.
Transitional vesicles: from the transitional ER to 
migrate and converge to cis face of Golgi
2.
Secretory vesicles: between the trans face of Golgi 
and the plasma membrane
3.
Clathrin-coated vesicles: play a role in intracellular 
traffic of membranes and of secretory products 
between ER and Golgi, between Golgi and the 
endosomal and lysosomal compartments.
Golgi structure
• Manufacturing and the shipping center of the cell.
• Under the electron microscope, the Golgi apparatus is 
seen to be composed of stacks of flattened structures 
that contain numerous vesicles containing secretory 
granules.
• It has a front end and a back end. The front end is called 
the cis face and the back end is called the trans face. 
• Pleomophic: compact and limited, in others 
spread out and reticular (net-like)
• Interconnecting tubules, vesicles, and cisternae.
Golgi function
• Sorting many of the cell’s proteins and membrane 
constituents, and in directing them to their proper 
destinations
• Packaging and exocytosis of the materials:
• Zymogen of exocrine pancreatic cells;
• Mucus (=a glycoprotein) secretion by goblet cells of the 
intestine
• Formation of melanin granules and other pigments
• Formation of certain cellular organelles such as 
plasma membrane, lysosomes, acrosome of 
spermatozoa
• Transport of lipid molecules
• Proteoglycans (PGs) are proteins modified by 
glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) in the Golgi apparatus
• Ribosomes are tiny spheroidal dense particles (of 
150 to 200 A0 diameters) that are primarily found in 
most prokaryotic and eukaryotic.
• Containing approximately equal amounts of rRNA 
and proteins 
• Prokaryotic cells: Ribosomes freely in the cytoplasm 
make proteins that will be utilized within the cell 
• Eukaryotic cells: ribosomes occur freely in the 
cytoplasm or remain attached to the outer surface of 
the ER membrane used for usage inside the cell or 
outside the cell.
Ribosomes
• Each ribosome is divided into two subunits:
1.
Small subunit: binds to a larger subunit and the mRNA 
pattern, and
2.
Large subunit: binds to the tRNA, the amino acids, and the 
smaller subunit.
• Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes = little subunit of 30S and the 
bigger subunit of 50S
• Eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes = little (40S) and substantial (60S) 
subunits
• During protein synthesis, when multiple ribosomes are attached to 
the same mRNA strand, this structure is known as 
poliribosomes/polysomes
• The existence of ribosomes is temporary
Ribosomes 
• The ribosomes in the chloroplasts and mitochondria of eukaryotes 
are comprised of big and little subunits composed of proteins inside a 
70S
Ribosomes function
• The site of biological protein synthesis 
(translation)
• Ribosomes link amino acids together in 
the order specified by messenger RNA 
(mRNA) molecules.
• Ribosomes act as catalysts in two 
extremely important biological 
processes called peptidyl transfer and 
peptidyl hydrolysis
Ribosomes: protein synthesis
• Dynamic & plastic
• Changing shape, diving and fusing
• Moving along microtubular cytoskeleton 
neuron, skeletal, cardiac muscle cell (between 
myofibril), sperm cell (around flagellum)
• Free or interact with ER (exchange lipid)
• Majority mitochondrial protein are encoded by 
nuclear genes & synthesis on cytosolic ribosomes
• Maternal inheritance
Mitochondria
• Double lipid bilayer
• Outer membrane: permeable to ion &                                                                                       
small molecule 5000 Da porin
• Inner membrane: 
• diffusion ion & small molecule, transport protein
• Contain large protein complexes of the 
respiratory chain
• Intermembrance space
• Cristae: oxidation phasphorylation cristae space. 
Proteins known as F0F1-ATPases that produce the 
majority of ATP used by cells are found distributed 
throughout the cristae.
• Mitochondrial matrix: contain 
• genetic system mtDNA nucleoids: 16 kn & 
encoded 13 protein-encoded genes; very limited 
repair of mtDNA; maternal pattern
• ribosom
A summary of the energy-converting metabolism in mitochondria
Glycolisis
Kreb’s cycle 
Rantai Transport Elektron
Kemiosmosis
Fosforilasi Oksidatif
Mitochondrial functioning in intermediary 
metabolism
• Carbohydrates, fats, amino acid 
metabolism
• Oxidative phosphorylation
• Krebs cycle
• Urea cycle
• Fatty acid oxidation
• Ketogenesis
• Triacylglicerol synthesis 
• Gluconeogenesis 
• Post translational modification 
• Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex 
(PDH): central to glucose 
metabolism
• Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)
• The ATP synthase
mitochondria
• Produce citrate & carbon component of the cells, fatty acids & 
sterol
• Membrane biosynthesis: phospholipid
• In starvation: protein amino acid mitochondria: NADH & ATP
• Liver cell: urea cycle amino acid ammonia (NH4+) urea: urin
• Biosynthesis of heme group
• Stability of the nuclear genome: iron-sulfur cluster
Mitochondria in apoptosis
• Extrinsic and intrinsic signal
• Outer membrane has attached a set 
of anti-apoptotic protein
• During the apoptosis: neutralization 
of anti-apoptotic protein by pro-
apoptotic protein cytochrome C, 
Bcl-2 family, AIF, endonuclease G, 
Smac and OMI/HtrA2 activate 
caspase cleavage protein & DNA 
degradation by macrophage & 
inflammatory cells
Mitochondrial destruction: mitophagy
• Mitochondrial disfunction Signal from mitochondria cytosol
chaperon activation & lysosome for degradation => mitochondrial 
retrograde signaling
• Organelle disfunction by altered ratio of ATP/ADP, Ca accumulation, 
ROS>>
• Removal of male sperm mitochondria on fertilization of an egg
• In the generation of erythrocytes, which lose their mitochondria 
before maturation
Mitochondrial in disease
• OXPHOS deficiencies 
• Etio: mutationof mtDNA or nuclear encoded genes
• the most common inborn errors of metabolism 
• incidence of 1 in 5,000
• Diversity of physiological phenotype:
• Lebers hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), mitochondrial 
encephalopathy, Kearn-Sayre syndrome, Leighs disease, progressive 
external opthalmoplegia, and neuropathy, ataxia and retinitis 
pigmentosa, cardiomyopathy and diabetes
OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION DEFICIENCIES
• During fasting or prolonged exercising
• Beta-oxidation (The degradation of fatty acids) defects
• Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia along with alterations in liver, heart, muscular 
and nervous systems
• Cancer preventing cell death
• The dysfunction BCl2 proteins 
• Cell proliferation and cancer induction
FATTY ACID OXIDATION DISORDERS
MITOCHONDRIA AND CANCER
• RNA viral infection
• Production of IFN-α and -β, and other pro-inflammatory cytokines
• Activates autophagy or apoptosis 
• Alzheimers disease (AD)reduced ATP production, increased free 
radical production, and increased apoptosis, reduced cytochrome c 
oxidase activity 
• Huntingtons diseasemutation of huntingtin protein (Htt) 
deficiency in oxidative metabolism and defects in mitochondrial 
Ca2+neuronal dysfunction in the striatum and cerebral cortex 
• Parkinsons disease: Complex I dysfunction superoxide production is 
broader in the substancia nigra 
MITOCHONDRIA IN THE INNATE IMMUNE RESPONSE
MITOCHONDRIA AND NEURODEGENERATION
• Self replicating organelles
• Single membrane
• Do not contain DNA or ribosom
• Protein are encoded in nucleus 
selective import from the cytosol
• Contain oxidative enzyme: catalase 
& oxidase
• Major site of oxygen utilization
• Peroxisome lowered the 
intracellular concentration of 
oxygen oxidation reaction
• No producing energy
Peroxisomes
• Use molecular oxygen to remove 
hydrogen atoms                                         
from specific organic substrates (~R) 
in an oxidation reaction that produce 
hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)
• Catalase uses the H2O2  to oxidase a 
variety of substrate  by the 
peroxidation reaction  & convert it to 
H2O (detoxication)
• Breakdown fatty acid molecule by β-
oxidation & convert it to acetyl CoA & 
then export it to cytosol
RH2 + O2 R + H2O2
2H2O2 2H2O + O2
Peroxixomes
• Biosynthetic function: plasmalogens >> phospholipid in myelin
• Plasmalogen deficiency: abnormalities in the myelination of nerve-cell 
axons neurological disease
• Protein signal located at the C-terminus is 3 amino acids (Ser-Lys-Leu) 
+ peroxin receptor on peroxisome membrane
• Protein do not have unfold to unfold to be imported
Mutation in the gene encoding peroxin Pex5 Defect 
importing protein into peroxisomes Zellwenger
syndrome: hypomyelination impaired neuronal 
migration, neuronal positioning & brain development
Other name: cerebrohepatorenal syndrome
A model that explain how peroxisome proliferate & 
how new peroxisomes arise
• Single membrane: keeps the cell itself from being digested
• 0.1–1.2 µm
• Their shape and size vary depending on what material is digested
• Mostly present in secretory cells: pancreatic cells, spleen cells, leucocytes
• Originate from Golgi cisternae or from the tubules of endoplasmic reticulum
• Containing digestive enzymes
• Uncontrolled release of lysosome contents into the cytoplasm can cause cell 
death (necrosis).
Suicide bag
Lysosomes: digestive enzyme
• Contain about 40 different hydrolytic 
enzymes:
• Lipase: digests lipids 
• Amylase: digest carbohydrates 
(e.g., sugars) 
• Proteases: digest proteins 
• Nucleases: digest nucleic acids 
• Filled with acid hydrolases work at 
low pH (highly acidic) levels 
• nucleases, proteases, glycosidases, 
lipases, phosphatases, sulfatases and 
phospholipases
Lysosome 
Secondary 
Primary 
Storage 
granule
Digestive 
vacuole
Residual 
bodies

vacuole
Lysosome function
1.
Digestion of ingested material from phagocytosis
• foreign invaders such as bacteria, food and old organelles 
• break them into small pieces that can hopefully 
• be used again
• fuses with the membrane of a food vacuole and squirts the enzymes inside.
• The digested food can then diffuse through the vacuole membrane and enter the 
cell to be used for energy or growth.
Lysosomes function
2. Autophagy & Cell Death
• Autolysis (self eating)
• Autophagosome  suicide bags of 
cell
• Programmed self-destruction
• Damage/ageing cell
• Enzyme release outside the cell to 
break down extracellular material
• Sperm release enzyme to dissolve 
protein coating ovum
